distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for a complex suppurative adnexal mass involving fallopian tube, ovary, and adjacent pelvic tissues. STI-associated, polymicrobial, anaerobic, enteric, IUD-associated, postpartum, post-procedure, postmenopausal, ruptured, bilateral, recurrent, and sepsis presentations remain mechanisms, axes, context modifiers, event hazards, source-control states, or future subtype layers rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume pelvic/lower abdominal pain, pelvic exam tenderness or discharge, systemic inflammatory response, and presentation imaging showing complex adnexal abscess/mass, pyosalpinx, fat stranding, free fluid, or adjacent-organ inflammation. Operative findings, drainage culture, pathology, final paper diagnosis, antimicrobial susceptibility, treatment response, and follow-up outcomes remain confirmatory or non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Upper genital tract or adjacent-source infection
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Microbial burden reaches the adnexa through ascending cervicovaginal/endometrial infection, postpartum or procedural tract disruption, IUD or foreign-body context, adjacent bowel or appendiceal inflammation, or less often hematogenous spread.

Mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms, including genital, enteric gram-negative, streptococcal, and anaerobic flora, sustain a low-oxygen pus compartment with variable culture yield and susceptibility context.
Salpingitis, oophoritis, pyosalpinx, phlegmon, and loculated pus coalesce into a complex adnexal inflammatory mass involving tube, ovary, and surrounding pelvic organs.

Inflamed adnexa and pus irritate pelvic peritoneum, cervix/uterus on bimanual exam, bowel, bladder, ureters, or abdominal wall planes, producing pain, tenderness, urinary or bowel symptoms, fat stranding, and reactive imaging changes.

Abscess burden, pelvic inflammation, bacteremia, rupture, or shock physiology drive fever, chills, tachycardia, leukocytosis, CRP/PCT rise, lactate, and organ-risk axes; fever or WBC can be blunted in older or immunosuppressed hosts.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Abscess size, pressure, and anatomic distortion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Large or bilateral collections distort pelvic anatomy, compress ureters or bowel/bladder, reduce antibiotic penetration, increase pain, and raise procedural source-control pressure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Abscess rupture, spillage, or anatomic spread
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Failure of containment can spill pus into the peritoneal cavity, cul-de-sac, bowel-adherent spaces, retroperitoneal or abdominal wall planes, causing peritonitis, shock, and urgent source-control need.
Undrained, multiloculated, inaccessible, ruptured, recurrent, or treatment-nonresponsive abscess maintains microbial and inflammatory activity despite antibiotics.

Concordant broad-spectrum antimicrobial exposure, anaerobic coverage, reliable absorption or IV exposure, drainage, operation, and adequate decompression reshape the vector field toward microbial clearance and resolving inflammation.
Severe adnexal inflammation and operation can damage tubal patency, ovarian reserve, and pelvic surfaces, creating infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, and recurrence risk.

Abscess burden can trigger systemic inflammation.
Large or multiloculated collections are harder to sterilize with antibiotics alone.
Uncontrolled abscess increases rupture, spillage, and extension risk.
Active broad-spectrum and anaerobic coverage lowers viable abscess burden.
Effective drainage or operation reduces uncontrolled source activity.
Source control and active coverage reduce ongoing spillage and peritonitis risk.
Severe adnexal inflammation damages tubes and pelvic surfaces over days to weeks.
Pelvic peritoneal irritation is the main pain driver.
Adnexal and pelvic inflammation often localizes to lower abdomen.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Bimanual tenderness axes co-occur from upper-genital-tract inflammation but can be incomplete.
Cervical discharge contributes to abnormal vaginal discharge but either may be absent.
Fever, pain, and inflammation commonly raise pulse.
WBC and CRP often rise together with abscess burden, though timing varies.
A larger measured complex adnexal collection implies present TOA activity.
TOA increases source-control pressure when large, ruptured, septic, or nonresponsive.
Larger collections are more likely to require and permit abscess-directed drainage, though access anatomy matters.
Rupture or pus spillage produces peritoneal irritation.
Diffuse peritonitis increases septic shock hazard.
Septic shock dominates near-term death risk.
Adequate drainage or operation lowers persistent sepsis and death hazard.
Adequate source control and lower persistent pelvic inflammation reduce chronic pain hazard; the direct adhesion mechanism edge is represented in mechanism_edges.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anaerobic coverage is important for abscess flora.
Antibiotics alone may be insufficient for large, ruptured, or nonresponding abscess.
Severe beta-lactam reaction limits cephalosporin use.

side_effects.interpretation: Doxycycline or metronidazole can worsen nausea.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral broad coverage vector for TOA while source-control need is assessed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cefoxitin or cefotetan provide anaerobic activity within PID/TOA regimens.

treatments.context_specific_role: Cephalosporin-based parenteral coverage vector where local availability and allergy context fit.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Beta-lactamase inhibitor coverage can fit mixed anaerobic abscess flora.
Severe beta-lactam reaction limits this path.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor vector for mixed pelvic abscess flora.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: This path may be used when beta-lactams are constrained.
Gentamicin requires renal dosing and toxicity monitoring.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative broad coverage vector when beta-lactam paths are constrained, with renal-toxicity context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Shock or severe sepsis increases value of rapid broad coverage.
Severe beta-lactam reaction constrains these agents.

failure_modes: carbapenem overuse in low resistance context
treatments.context_specific_role: Broad severe-infection vector when septic physiology, resistant gram-negative risk, or adjacent enteric source context is high.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vomiting, ileus, shock, or malabsorption makes oral completion unreliable.
Oral therapy cannot compensate for persistent undrained source.

treatments.context_specific_role: Completion vector after clinical improvement, adequate coverage, and source-control trajectory are established.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: A drainable collection is required for drainage to reshape source control.
Unsafe or nonvisualized access lowers procedural effect.
Bleeding risk changes drainage safety.

side_effects.interpretation: Drainage bleeding risk depends on access route and coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control vector for drainable TOA, large collection, nonresponse, or sepsis physiology.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Diffuse peritonitis increases value of urgent operative control.
Shock requires rapid source control plus resuscitation.
Operation only helps if pus and infected tissue are controlled.

side_effects.interpretation: Operative blood loss and dilution can lower hemoglobin.

treatments.context_specific_role: Operative vector for ruptured TOA, diffuse peritonitis, failed drainage, bowel involvement, diagnostic uncertainty with surgical emergency, or life-threatening sepsis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Shock physiology increases benefit of fluids, vasopressors, monitoring, and ICU support.
Resuscitation supports physiology but does not sterilize or drain the source.

treatments.context_specific_role: Physiologic support for hypotension, tachycardia, AKI risk, or shock while antimicrobial and source-control vectors address the cause.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Symptom improvement alone should not be interpreted as abscess control.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive symptom vector with serial examination and reassessment; not a substitute for active coverage or source control.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Recent exposure raises upper-tract infection prior context.
Chlamydia exposure changes coverage context.
Gonorrhea remains relevant while testing is pending.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior and STI-coverage context without requiring positive NAAT.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: BV-associated anaerobes participate in pelvic abscess flora.
Anaerobic context increases value of anaerobic coverage.
Prior inflammation increases adhesions and recurrence context.
Prior pelvic damage raises chronic pain risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises recurrence and sequela context without hardcoding diagnosis.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: IUD context is a local risk and source context in selected TOA cases.
Long-duration retained devices can be associated with pelvic inflammatory masses.

present.trajectory_modulation: Adds device-source context without making IUD-associated TOA a separate disease name.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Recent delivery, abortion, or uterine procedure changes source context.
Mucosal disruption can facilitate infection.
Postpartum or procedural pelvic infection can be polymicrobial and anaerobic.

present.trajectory_modulation: Shifts source and organism context while remaining within TOA.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Adjacent bowel or bladder inflammation can either mimic or contribute to TOA.
Enteric context increases gram-negative/anaerobic coverage importance.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises mimic competition and enteric-source coverage context; does not override appendicitis or diverticulitis leaves.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Large or persistent abscess increases drainage or surgery pressure.
Large abscess and nonresponse raise rupture risk.
Complicated abscess phenotypes increase near-term risk.
Rupture produces peritonitis.
Rupture and uncontrolled source increase shock risk.
Shock and peritonitis dominate near-term mortality.

present.trajectory_modulation: Moves trajectory into urgent antimicrobial, resuscitation, and source-control regime.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Adnexal mass in postmenopause requires malignancy and ovarian tumor fairness checks.
Older age and comorbidity raise severe infection and operative risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises mimic competition and reserve risk without making malignancy a TOA label.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Fever can be absent despite severe infection.
Lower host reserve raises severe infection hazard.
Comorbidity increases kidney vulnerability.

present.trajectory_modulation: Can blunt classic inflammatory signs while increasing complication and treatment-toxicity risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy is a treatment-safety, ectopic-mimic, and disposition context.
Maternal morbidity and obstetric risk lower tolerance for outpatient or unsafe treatment paths.

present.trajectory_modulation: Pregnancy changes treatment and monitoring context rather than defining the leaf.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Missed source control sustains burden and rupture/shock hazard.
Uncontrolled source and delayed active therapy worsen outcomes.

present.trajectory_modulation: Prolongs disease until active coverage and source control are achieved.

supportive_care: Structure presentation pelvic evidence directly: pelvic pain, lower abdominal localization, cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, discharge, pelvic mass, peritoneal signs, and systemic inflammatory labs are observed axes, not diagnosis labels.

Use pelvic ultrasound, CT, or MRI findings when available: complex adnexal mass, TOA size, pyosalpinx or hydrosalpinx, fat stranding, pelvic free fluid, adjacent bowel/bladder involvement, hydronephrosis, rupture, and extraperitoneal extension should be mapped as axes.

Keep operative findings, drainage culture species, susceptibility, pathology, final paper diagnosis, and improvement after antibiotics/drainage in confirmatory or post-workup fields for presentation-only ranking.
Culture and NAAT results reshape organism and treatment context; negative cervical gonorrhea/chlamydia testing should not erase TOA when imaging and pelvic findings support an upper-tract abscess.

Assess pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ovarian tumor, appendicitis, diverticulitis, pyelonephritis, postpartum endometritis, septic abortion, and sepsis fairly when their observed axes are present.

Source control is a state variable: abscess size, multiloculation, rupture, diffuse peritonitis, shock, nonresponse to antibiotics, feasibility of drainage, and operative risk determine whether drainage or operation reshapes RMST.
Partner management and STI public-health steps affect reinfection and exposure context but should not be encoded as semantic priority labels.
quality_notes: Tubo-ovarian abscess was distilled from the disease name alone; pathogen, rupture, postpartum status, and sepsis are represented as mechanisms, axes, modifiers, or event hazards.
No treatment priority-label fields are used.
